newsitem.title: GERMANY: German nuclear ritual unleashes row over who pays.
newsitem.headline: German nuclear ritual unleashes row over who pays.

text.p: As a controversial nuclear waste shipment made its way to a storage dump on Wednesday, Germans performed what has become an annual ritual with security forces and anti-nuclear demonstrators locked in confrontation.

In Germany's biggest post-war security operation to ensure spent fuel rods reached Gorleben storage depot safely, some 30,000 police were pitted against thousands of protesters opposed to the transportation of nuclear waste.
Although some are militants bent on violent disruption, the vast majority are peaceful and appear to be from a cross-section of Germany's environmentally-conscious society.
This third year of protests aimed at blocking shipments to Gorleben have drawn increased support but also incurred more costs for cash-strapped local authorities.
This year's transport is expected to cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million) and surpass the 46 million marks spent on bringing a smaller shipment to Gorleben last year.
The high costs have fuelled an already simmering row over financing.

Bavarian Environment Minister Thomas Goppel criticised security forces in Lower Saxony, where Gorleben is located, for not being tough enough on protesters after some used quick-drying cement to lock their arms under railway tracks and masked militants threw petrol bombs at riot police.

But Lower Saxony Interior Minister Gerhard Glogowski argued that regions with atomic power stations, such as Bavaria, should take responsibility for their own nuclear waste or at least help pay for its delivery.

"It's outrageous for Goppel to say border guards have failed to do their duty," Glogowski told ZDF television. "If he had kept the nuclear waste there and stored it in a reasonable way we wouldn't have had these problems in the first place."
Gorleben is Germany's main medium-term nuclear waste storage facility and a permanent waste dump is also planned there.

But the Social Democrat (SPD) state government in Lower Saxony, responsible for overseeing the dump and ensuring the safety of nuclear waste consignments, is anxious that the nuclear waste burden be shared.
It wants states such as Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg in the south, where a high proportion of Germany's nuclear power plants are sited, to develop their own waste dumps as well.
The SPD wants Germany to begin what it admits will be a long-term exit from nuclear power as an energy source.
As a member of the SPD government, Glogowski is torn between his party's firm anti-nuclear stance while being forced to send in thousands of police to guard the nuclear shipments.
And he is not the only one going through the motions of the annual confrontation.
"If I had the choice I would rather demonstrate than be sent here to defend the nuclear waste shipments," police officer Tanja Braeutigam, 22, told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
"Phone in sick," protesters shouted at the tall woman officer clad in full riot gear.
"I will not let them push me about," she said of the jeering crowd, who sense some police sympathise with their cause.
She said she hoped the government would put a stop to nuclear waste shipments so that such security operations were not necessary.
